subject: Mixed
description: Medium-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Anatomy, Biochemistry, Fundamentals of Electro Therapy, Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiology, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: In manual muscle testing, the 'break test' is best described as:

options.A: Applying resistance throughout an actively moving joint to see when motion ceases
options.B: Bringing the part to the end of its available range and asking the patient to hold that position while the therapist tries to force ('break') it out of position
options.C: Passively moving a joint until tissue resistance is felt
options.D: Timing how long a muscle can sustain a maximal isometric hold

questions.explanation: The break test — the most commonly used MMT procedure — has the patient hold the end-range test position while the therapist applies gradually increasing resistance, attempting to 'break' the hold. The alternative 'active resistance test' (resisting throughout the motion) requires more skill and is not generally recommended because results are often equivocal.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: According to the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification of breathlessness, a patient who becomes symptomatic with mild exertion such as bathing or dressing falls into which class?

options.A: Class I
options.B: Class II
options.C: Class III
options.D: Class IV

questions.explanation: NYHA Class III describes symptoms occurring with mild exertion (e.g. bathing, showering, dressing). Class I is asymptomatic except with severe exertion, Class II is symptomatic with ordinary activity (e.g. walking upstairs), and Class IV is symptomatic even at rest.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Breathlessness Classification
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: What is the key limitation of Sanger's reagent (1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene) compared to Edman's reagent for determining a protein's amino acid sequence?

options.A: It only works on carbohydrates, not proteins
options.B: After labelling the N-terminal residue, the protein must be fully hydrolysed to identify it — destroying the polypeptide and preventing repeated sequencing cycles
options.C: It cannot label any amino acid at all
options.D: It is more expensive but otherwise functionally identical to Edman's reagent

questions.explanation: Sanger's reagent labels the free N-terminal amino group, but identifying that labelled residue requires complete hydrolysis of the protein — destroying it in the process. This makes it useful only for identifying the N-terminal residue once, unlike Edman degradation which can be repeated.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure
questions.subject: Biochemistry

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Impulses with a duration of less than 10 ms, used for stimulating normal (innervated) muscle, are classified as having:

options.A: A long duration, termed interrupted direct current
options.B: A short duration, of the faradic type
options.C: No classification exists for pulse duration
options.D: A duration only used for denervated muscle

questions.explanation: Impulses of less than 10 ms duration are classed as short duration and are of the faradic type, used to stimulate normal innervated muscle via its motor nerve, typically repeated at a high rate of 50-100 per second.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A patient's gluteus medius is graded 4 (Good) on manual muscle testing. Which functional finding is consistent with this grade, per Daniels and Worthingham's discussion of why 'Good' is not always good enough?

options.A: Completely normal, symmetric gait with no compensation
options.B: A positive Trendelenburg sign during single-leg stance
options.C: Complete inability to abduct the hip against gravity
options.D: No palpable or visible muscle contraction at all

questions.explanation: Even a 'Good' (Grade 4) gluteus medius can be functionally inadequate — a positive Trendelenburg sign (contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance) can still appear, illustrating the gap between a manual muscle grade and real functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Why is establishing a 1-RM (single maximum effort) considered inappropriate for certain patient populations, such as those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology?

options.A: It takes too long to administer in a clinical setting
options.B: It requires a single maximal effort, which carries risk for patients with joint impairments, healing soft tissue, osteoporosis, or cardiovascular pathology
options.C: It is only valid for measuring endurance, not strength
options.D: It cannot be performed using free weights

questions.explanation: A 1-RM test requires the patient to exert one true maximal effort, which is unsafe for patients with joint impairments, those recovering from or at risk of soft tissue injury, or those with osteoporosis or cardiovascular pathology — alternative methods (e.g. multiple-RM formulas, dynamometry, percentage of body weight) are used instead for these patients.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Repetition Maximum, Precautions
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign is performed with the patient supine, knee flexed 80-90°, hip flexed 45°, and the foot slightly medially rotated. A positive test (excessive posterior movement/rotation of the medial tibia) is most indicative of injury to which primary structure?

options.A: Anterior cruciate ligament in isolation
options.B: Posterior cruciate ligament (along with posteromedial supporting structures)
options.C: Lateral collateral ligament only
options.D: Iliotibial band

questions.explanation: A positive Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign indicates injury to the posterior cruciate ligament, along with possible involvement of the posterior oblique ligament, medial collateral ligament, semimembranosus, and posteromedial capsule — it tests for posteromedial rotary instability of the knee.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Ligament Stability, Posteromedial and Posterolateral Drawer Sign
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In the 'dual process theory' of clinical reasoning, 'Type 1' thinking is best described as:

options.A: Slow, deliberate, and highly analytical
options.B: Intuitive, fast, automatic, and pattern-recognition based, but more vulnerable to error
options.C: Used exclusively by inexperienced clinicians
options.D: A thinking style with no relevance to medical practice

questions.explanation: Type 1 thinking is intuitive, heuristic, automatic, fast, and effortless — highly efficient (used in roughly 95% of daily decisions) but more vulnerable to error and more affected by context than Type 2 thinking, which is slow, deliberate, and analytical.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Type 1 and Type 2 Thinking
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Why does ischaemia (reduced blood/oxygen supply) lead to cell swelling and damage?

options.A: Ischaemia has no effect on the Na+-K+ pump
options.B: Ischaemia decreases Na+-K+ pump activity, disrupting osmotic equilibrium and allowing the cell to swell
options.C: Ischaemia directly ruptures the cell membrane through mechanical force
options.D: Ischaemia only affects extracellular fluid, never intracellular volume

questions.explanation: The Na+-K+ pump normally keeps osmotic equilibrium by moving positive charge (and effectively solute) out of the cell, counteracting the tendency of intracellular protein anions and other molecules to draw water in and cause swelling. Ischaemia reduces the ATP-dependent pump's activity, disrupting this balance — which is why prolonged cerebral ischaemia, causing cell swelling and damage, is often fatal.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Gibbs-Donnan Effect
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: A fall on the outstretched hand causing tenderness in the anatomical snuff box most classically suggests a fracture of which carpal bone?

options.A: Lunate
options.B: Pisiform
options.C: Scaphoid
options.D: Hamate

questions.explanation: Scaphoid fracture is common after a fall on the outstretched hand and classically presents with tenderness and swelling in the anatomical snuff box, plus pain on longitudinal percussion of the thumb and index finger.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The lateral surface of the pisiform bone is grooved by which structure?

options.A: The radial artery
options.B: The median nerve
options.C: The ulnar nerve
options.D: The tendon of flexor carpi radialis

questions.explanation: The lateral surface of the pisiform is grooved by the ulnar nerve as it passes into the hand through Guyon's canal, alongside the ulnar artery.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: Closed-chain exercise is best described as exercise performed:

options.A: In a nonweight-bearing position with the distal segment moving freely
options.B: In a weight-bearing position where the body moves over a fixed distal segment
options.C: Only using free weights, never body weight
options.D: Exclusively with the upper extremity

questions.explanation: Closed-chain exercise is performed in a weight-bearing position, where the body moves over a relatively fixed distal segment (e.g. the foot on the ground during a squat). Open-chain exercise, by contrast, is performed nonweight-bearing, with the distal segment (hand or foot) moving freely.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Position for Exercise
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Training to improve muscular (local) endurance typically involves:

options.A: A very heavy load for only 1-2 repetitions
options.B: Many repetitions (e.g. 3-5 sets of 40-50 reps) against a low, submaximal load
options.C: A single maximal isometric contraction held for 1 second
options.D: Complete rest with no muscular activity

questions.explanation: Muscle endurance training involves performing many repetitions against a submaximal load — for example, as many as three to five sets of 40 to 50 repetitions against a low resistance — and can be safely initiated early in rehabilitation since the load involved is low.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — To Improve Muscle Endurance
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Social phobia is characterised primarily by fear of:

options.A: Open or crowded spaces
options.B: One's own actions being critically viewed by others, leading to embarrassment or humiliation
options.C: A single specific, well-circumscribed object like spiders or heights
options.D: Contamination by dirt or germs

questions.explanation: Social phobia is an irrational fear of performing activities in front of others or interacting socially, driven by fear that one's own actions will be judged critically, leading to embarrassment (examples include fear of public speaking, blushing, or eating in front of others).
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Phobic Disorder
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Despite his severe memory problems, patient H.M. had relatively normal short-term memory (e.g. could repeat six numbers forward after hearing them once) and intact memories from before his operation. What was specifically impaired?

options.A: His ability to form new long-term memories
options.B: His personality and IQ, both of which dropped sharply
options.C: His sense of touch and vision
options.D: His ability to speak or understand language

questions.explanation: H.M.'s deficit was specifically in forming new long-term memories (anterograde amnesia) — his immediate/short-term memory and his remote memories from before the surgery were largely preserved, illustrating that short-term and long-term memory, and the process of consolidating one into the other, are at least partly separable.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Memory Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Faradic-type currents are typically 'surged' for treatment purposes. What is the purpose of surging the current?

options.A: To reduce the total treatment time
options.B: To produce a near-normal tetanic-like contraction and relaxation of the muscle, by gradually increasing then decreasing the intensity of successive impulses
options.C: To eliminate the need for any electrodes
options.D: To convert the current into direct current permanently

questions.explanation: Surging gradually increases the intensity of successive impulses to a peak, then lets it fall (suddenly or gradually), mimicking a more natural, near-normal tetanic muscle contraction and relaxation cycle rather than an abrupt on/off stimulus.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Modified Faradic Currents
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: 'Overconfidence bias' in clinical decision-making refers to:

options.A: The tendency to always order more diagnostic tests than necessary
options.B: The tendency to believe one knows more than one actually does, placing too much faith in opinion over gathered evidence
options.C: A bias that only affects junior doctors, never senior clinicians
options.D: Excessive reliance on clinical prediction rules

questions.explanation: Overconfidence bias is the tendency to place too much faith in one's own opinion rather than the gathered evidence, sometimes compounded further by availability bias and commission bias (a tendency to act rather than not act), occasionally with serious consequences.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Common Cognitive Biases
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: The concept of a 'treatment threshold' in clinical decision-making primarily balances:

options.A: The doctor's personal preference against the hospital's budget
options.B: The risks of testing/waiting against the risks and benefits of starting treatment now
options.C: Only the cost of the test, with no consideration of patient risk
options.D: Nothing — treatment thresholds do not exist in evidence-based medicine

questions.explanation: The treatment threshold combines the risks of a test, and the risks versus benefits of treatment, to decide the point at which it makes sense to act. For a low-risk, effective intervention (e.g. antibiotics for a likely UTI), the threshold to act is lower; for a high-risk intervention, more diagnostic certainty is required first.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Dealing with Uncertainty
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: What is the general relationship between the intensity (load) of resistance exercise and the number of repetitions/sets possible?

options.A: There is no relationship — repetitions are independent of load
options.B: An inverse relationship: higher intensity/load permits fewer repetitions and sets, and lower load permits more
options.C: A direct relationship: higher load always allows more repetitions
options.D: Repetitions only depend on the patient's age, never on the load used

questions.explanation: There is an inverse relationship between exercise intensity (load) and the number of repetitions/sets possible — the higher the load, the fewer repetitions and sets that can be performed, and vice versa.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Volume
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: The hypothalamus regulates the body's internal environment (temperature, blood salt concentration, hormone levels) chiefly by controlling secretions from which gland?

options.A: The thyroid gland
options.B: The pituitary gland
options.C: The adrenal gland directly, bypassing the pituitary entirely
options.D: The pancreas

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus is connected to the pituitary gland and controls its hormone secretion into the bloodstream, either through nerve impulses or chemical releasing factors — linking the nervous system to the body's broader glandular (endocrine) system.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Forebrain: Hypothalamus and Pituitary
questions.subject: Psychology
